utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60/1-S, the Prosecutor versus Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a sentencing hearing for Mr. Momir Nikolic in accordance with Rule 100 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal, as well as a decision rendered by this Trial Chamber October 6th, 2003. Before we start, could we have the appearances, please. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Peter McCloskey, and I'm accompanied by Stefan Waespi, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For Mr. Momir Nikolic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, do we have the interpretation? I think there's some technical problems. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please try it again, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Appearing for Mr. Momir Nikolic are myself, his lead counsel, Veselin Londrovic, and my esteemed colleague, co-counsel Stefan Kirsch, attorney at law from Frankfurt, and with us is our interpreter, Ms. Vesna Anic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can, and I understand the language spoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you have anything to complain during your stay in the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I have no complaints. There are no problems as regards the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we'll have the sentencing hearing. As we understand, that both parties submitted their sentencing briefings, as well as the supplementary submissions already, so I'll give each party about 20 to 30 minutes to brief the Court the highlights of their briefings. Shall we start from the Prosecution? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I have stated earlier in this -- in this court, it is not my intention at this time to go at length into the Srebrenica case. This Court is fully aware of that case. And we are here today because Mr. Nikolic has chosen to admit the facts in the indictment and plead guilty. And the Prosecution will be relying in part on what he said when he testified as the factual basis for this guilty plea, as well as the few testimonies from the record of a previous trial. And I would like at the -- to say some remarks at the end of this proceedings as my remarks now will -- will be brief. We know that this Srebrenica case involves the forcible transportation, the forcible removal, the ethnic cleansing of the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica and the operation to separate, detain, and murder over 7.000 Muslim men from that enclave. Many of the facts of that case have been spoken to in bitter and stark detail by Mr. Nikolic himself, but today I will briefly go over some of the -- the facts, the statements of the four people that we have offered the Court that I believe are a representative sampling. We did not want to bring anyone to the great and terrible burden of coming all the way from their home and again having to speak of these events. We believe 92 bis was specifically designed for this kind of thing and -- and so we have not chosen to put on what may typically in an adversarial process be a long hearing where we pour out the entire facts of the crime. But I will just briefly remind you what some of these witnesses had to say. Let's start with Lieutenant Van Duijn, the Dutch lieutenant who was on duty at the time, from the 10th, the 12th, through the 13th of July. And as you'll recall, he witnessed the -- the shelling of the -- of the civilian population and the -- and their flight to Potocari, and he witnessed the fear in their eyes and in their being and he saw the separations of the men and the women, and he -- and he told about that. He's told about that over and over again. I think his testimony is a -- is a good representative sample of what the Dutch soldiers saw and what they can provide. You'll recall he made a comment that he thought he was -- he was watching a combination of two movies, Sophie's Choice and Schindler's List. I guess we can be thankful that his generation of soldiers has to refer to movies to recount the horrors of World War II, but it does remind us that -- that Srebrenica was and is the worst massacre coming out of Europe since that time, and his testimony and others like him help the world to see that, but of course, did so Momir Nikolic's. Another person that we know as Witness DD, a Muslim woman who was at Potocari and who vividly describe it is separation of her 15-year-old boy from her represents the -- one of the greatest tragedies of this case, the -- the mothers that were left behind that without their men, without their boys, and what horror they went through. Then we have Witness I. You may recall he's a Muslim man, a rather elderly fellow that was separated from his sons, from his family at Potocari. He was no threat to anyone. He was detained in Potocari, then he was detained in Bratunac for at least two days, subjected to the -- to horrors of that detention in Bratunac. And then he, along with thousands of others, was bussed out to the Zvornik area, where he was taken to the Branjevo military farm and subjected to the mass execution of over 1.000 people at the Branjevo farm, where he survived, he and others survived to tell us about it. And one -- just a reminder of his -- of his testimony, at the end, which perhaps he gives some of us some reason to hope, because he told us the story of a -- I think it was a Serb waiter, somewhere around Zvornik, that helped him out and gave him some soup and someone that he'll never forget because out of all this horror and all this ethnic strife here was at least one man that was willing to help his brother. And for a man like this, an old fellow, to be able to get up and tell his tale and tell his -- what happened to him and end it with that -- with that -- that event at that little cafe in and around Zvornik is -- gives us, I think, some reason to hope, as this plea agreement does and what has happened here today, what has brought us here today. Our last 92 bis witness is a psychologist, a Muslim psychologist from Tuzla, Teofika Ibrahimefendic [phoen], who reminds us and tell us of the difficulty that the women and survivors of Srebrenica had to go through and are still going through to this very day. And it's important to remember what she said about that and how it's different from other -- what other families and other victims of this war went through, and it's different because the scale was so massive and that the numbers of the Muslim men from the families were taken away and that these women are left, in her words, with perpetual uncertainty about what would happen to them and that is something that they would never recover from. And she goes on to describe how that was particularly difficult on the children. And she describes one particular instance where a boy was pointed at by a soldier and -- in Potocari and -- and was told that -- and the mother said, "Oh, he's only eight years old. Don't take him. Don't take him," and the soldier said, "If he was ten years old, he would be separated." And of course, this boy to this very day is afraid and lives in fear from being separated, from being taken away. So I think these -- these four witnesses are a representative of this case and are a reminder of the horror, the breadth, the scope of this crime, but I would also point out to you the testimony of Momir Nikolic, his admissions, his acknowledgments, and compare it to what you know, what else -- what other information you know and consider it as you consider the sentence. But at this time, I would like to -- I think it would be more appropriate to direct my comments regarding cooperation to the end, when it would be more in context. But I can say now that, as you know, we are here pursuant to the plea agreement, and it was -- this plea agreement was contingent upon the full cooperation of Mr. Nikolic, and it is the view of the Prosecution that he has cooperated fully with the Prosecution and that his testimony at trial was credible and that in looking at his testimony you need to compare the testimony of other witnesses in the overall programme to finally determine it for yourselves. But the Prosecution is satisfied that he has met his obligation, and we stand by that agreement and we recommend that based on that agreement, he should face a sentence of between 15 and 20 years. And at the end of these hearings, I would like to explain why I feel that his cooperation is so valuable and why these -- this term of years is appropriate in a situation and in a case as serious as this. I think it would be better if that was explained at the end. But, of course, I can -- I always am available to answer any questions the Court has on this agreement and Mr. Nikolic's cooperation in it.
