utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you. The Bench has a question to you, Mr. McCloskey. In your sentencing brief and mitigating factor, the section "Cooperation with the Prosecution," the Prosecution indicated that "Mr. Nikolic has provided the valuable information for the trial of Blagojevic and Jokic, an ongoing investigation into events of Srebrenica, including the specific locations of two hitherto unknown mass graves in the Srebrenica area." Could you elaborate on this point? Was one of the graves Black Peak, or Crni Vrh, which may be one of the largest mass graves yet discovered?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't believe that the graves that were identified by Mr. Nikolic was the grave that has been commonly referred to as Crni Vrh, which is in the Zvornik Brigade zone of responsibility, as far as I know. And I believe that grave is from the ethnic cleansing of 1992. The graves that Mr. Nikolic identified were in the area south of Potocari, in the back country there, in the -- in a similar area where other secondary mass graves were. We've identified some eight or nine secondary mass graves from the Glogova grave site, the Glogova grave site being the victims from the Kravica warehouse, some -- at least 1.000 victims from the Kravica warehouse and from other killings that may have occurred along the road. These -- these graves -- this grave at Glogova was disturbed in the end of September and October by the VRS forces, and they were buried in separate graves roughly containing between 100 and 200 people each in the road near Zeleni Jadar, which is just outside the Srebrenica enclave, some 10 or 20 miles south of Srebrenica. The graves that were identified by Mr. Nikolic are closer, I believe are between Srebrenica and Potocari, and he was able to point to us on a -- on a good military map where these sites were, and he -- we were able to, with the assistance of -- of some governments and getting aerial imagery under Rule 70, were able to identify disturbed earth in those specific locations. This is the -- one to have traditional methods that we had identified graves before. We are -- we have been working with the international community. We have gone to those sites. We have identified them as -- as -- as grave sites, but we have yet to have been able to receive the authorisation to put a shovel in them. And though everything I know at this point indicates to me that this is disturbed soil that occurred at the time of the events in question and it appears very much like a mass grave, and I can provide you more information on that, but I would prefer to go into private session very briefly, if you want any more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now I turn to the Defence for Mr. Nikolic. Do you have any opening remarks at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Defence understands these sentencing proceedings properly for Mr. Momir Nikolic, it is our view that the -- at the end of the sentencing proceedings we shall have an opportunity to make an oral closing statement after the Defence witnesses have been heard and exhibits tendered, part of which we have already submitted, but in the meantime we have gathered some more documents. So I would not like to waste time now, in order to avoid repeating myself, I wish to say that in its closing statement, the Defence will draw attention to the key elements of our written sentencing brief. Therefore, I ask Your Honour to allow me over the next ten minutes only to tell you very briefly what it is the Defence intends to do during the sentencing proceedings. If I understand these proceedings correctly, please allow me to present in brief what it is the Defence plans to do during this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the sentencing hearing for Mr. Nikolic, the Defence intends to call four witnesses who will testify viva voce, and they will speak about the personality and character of Mr. Momir Nikolic up to the outbreak of war on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Defence had intended to call a fifth witness, and protective measures had already been granted for that witness, who had the pseudonym DC, but for objective reasons this witness was unable to travel to The Hague. He had a prostate operation and is now recovering. In this sentencing hearing, the Defence further intends to tender certain documents, most of which Your Honours have already received together with the sentencing brief. And I believe there will not be any problems with accepting these exhibits. They are marked A1 to A14 in our brief. I will briefly tell you what documents these are. These are excerpts from the register of marriages and births for Mr. Momir Nikolic and his wife, Dusanka, excerpts from the register of births for Mr. Nikolic's two sons, and his mother, Mrs. Milenija Nikolic. Further, there are documents showing what Mrs. Dusanka Nikolic's salary is, Momir Nikolic's wife, and the amount of the pension received by his mother. Further, the Defence wishes to tender a written statement by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Ken Corlett, which shows to what extent Mr. Nikolic cooperated before his arrest. Further, there is a statement by the Bratunac police station certifying that Mr. Momir Nikolic was never previously convicted of any crime. Further, there is a certificate from the Srebrenica court and the Bijeljina district court, and these are the courts with subject matter and territorial jurisdiction according to the laws of Republika Srpska certifying that no criminal proceedings have been instituted against Mr. Momir Nikolic for any crime. Further, there is a report on the behaviour of Mr. Momir Nikolic in the Detention Unit, and in the forthcoming proceedings the Defence intends to present to the Court three further documents, one of which is a letter of the current mayor of the Srebrenica municipality. And when one reads this letter, one can see that the current mayor of the Srebrenica municipality absolutely supports the admission of guilt and acceptance of responsibility by Mr. Momir Nikolic. The following document that the Defence intends to present to the Trial Chamber is an article from the Wall Street magazine, the European edition of that magazine, which is entitled "Comments and views," and the article demonstrates -- or rather, the contents of the article demonstrate that the Prosecution has made significant progress with respect to establishing the truth about the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, and they managed to make this progress when they obtained a plea agreement with Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic. This article also shows that for a long time now public opinion has been expecting them to appear before this Tribunal. They have been expecting such important and credible witnesses to appear before this Tribunal, witnesses such as Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic. And the third document, the third document that the Defence will present to the Trial Chamber is an article from the New York Times, which is entitled "Truth of The Hague." And in our opinion, it is a very important article, as it was written by one of the victims of the events, of the crimes perpetrated in Srebrenica in July 1995, and this victim expresses himself in very affirmative manners with regard to the plea of guilty entered by Mr. Nikolic. Before I call the first witness for the Defence, who has not requested protective measures, I - the witness is Mr. Milorad Krsmanovic - I would like to request the Trial Chamber to allow Mr. Stefan Kirsch, co-counsel, to give a brief clarification of a paragraph in our sentencing brief, which we have submitted -- which we submitted on the 14th of July of this year to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Londrovic. One -- just one question: As for those documents, are you going to tender them through the live witness or as 92 bis documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I intend to tender them through the witness, a witness who in the Defence's opinion will also speak in positive terms about the guilty plea of Mr. Nikolic. I think that there is no doubt to be cast on these pieces of evidence and that the Prosecution will have no objection, since we have already discussed these documents with our colleagues from the Prosecution, and they didn't express any concern or any doubts about this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kirsch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I just draw Your Honours' attention to our sentencing brief. I refer to page 14, and the court file is page 91, paragraph 38. There it reads, the first sentence: "Mr. Nikolic did not voluntarily surrender since he was not aware of the sealed indictment and did know that an indictment against him was issued only a few days before his arrest." When I went through this document some days ago, it would appeared to me that probably it should read, adding another "not" before the second "know," so it would read "Mr. Nikolic did not voluntary surrender since he was not aware of the sealed indictment and did not" - this would be the change - "know that an indictment against him was only a few days before his arrest." I hope that it was clear what we went to say in that. And the second minor issue was in the sentence it said, "An indictment against him was issued only a few days ago." More properly, it should read, "was confirmed a few days ago,".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're at the stage of dealing with the evidence. Mr. McCloskey, for the sake of the record, are you sure that you're not going to call any live witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am sure I do not intend to call any live witnesses. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And how about those written statements? Are they -- are you going to tender them through the 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Those were statements of a previous trial, 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection from Defence counsel? Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I have understood my colleague from the Prosecution well, if we are referring to the written statements that we have already received with the written submission, with the sentencing brief, if that is what is in question, we have no objections to make to those written statements. If it doesn't concern anything new, if it only concerns those statements, we have no objection to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's the statements of the four witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. If there's no objections from the Defence team, we decided that those four statements are admitted into evidence at this stage. Now could we have the first witness, please. Well, while waiting for the witness, the scheduling for this afternoon is that we will make a break at 4.30 for 30 minutes and that we'll resume at 5.00 and sit for another 90 minutes until 6.30. We hope we could finish the four witnesses on the list today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, my name is Veselin Londrovic. I represent the accused, Mr. Momir Nikolic. And on behalf of the accused, Mr. Momir Nikolic, I will be putting a certain number of questions to you, which mainly concern your statement which you gave to Mr. Nikolic's Defence counsel. To ensure that the Trial Chamber knows which statement is concerned, it's been designated as TBB1 and attached -- and it is attached to our sentencing brief. Since we speak the same language, I would like to ask you to first make sure that you have heard my question and to wait for the end of the interpretation. You will hear when the interpreter has finished interpreting the question. Then you could answer my question to facilitate the interpreter's task. Have we understood each other?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, could you tell this Trial Chamber your first and last name, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milorad Krsmanovic. I was born on the 26th of August, 1954 in Repovac in the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: And what is your nationality, Mr. Krsmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which university you graduated from and what subject you studied.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I finished the University of -- I graduated from the University of Forestry, and my profession is -- by profession I'm a forestry engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you live at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I now live in Repovac, in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, do you know Mr. Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell this Trial Chamber in greater detail since when you have known Mr. Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have known Momir Nikolic for almost my entire life, since Momir and I live close to each other. We grew up together, and we socialised throughout our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell this Trial Chamber how far it is from your house to Mr. Momir Nikolic's house.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: About 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, you said that you were about a year older than Mr. Nikolic. Did you go to the same primary school? Did you go to the primary school that Mr. Nikolic went to at the same time and to the same secondary school at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We went to primary school together, but Mr. Momir Nikolic was in a lower class because he was one year younger. I went to secondary school in Ljubovija and Mr. Momir Nikolic went to secondary school in Bratunac, engineering secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, did you study together with Mr. Nikolic in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We studied in Sarajevo at the same time, but Momir studied general national defence and I studied forestry, but we would often see each other in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that when Mr. Nikolic finished the University of National Defence he returned to Bratunac and found employment there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After he had graduated, he returned to Bratunac and found a job in the secondary school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell this Trial Chamber what Mr. Nikolic did exactly in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He taught a subject called general national defence in the secondary school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, did Mr. Nikolic get married? And if he did, do you know his wife's name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He got married, and his wife's name is Dusanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any sons? Did Mr. Momir Nikolic and Dusanka have any sons? And if they did, do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Momir and Dusanka Nikolic have two sons. The elder one is called Branislav, and the younger one is called Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: If you know anything about this, could you tell the Trial Chamber what Branislav and Aleksandar do.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The elder son, Branislav, is studying in Belgrade, and the younger son, Aleksandar, is going to school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, does Momir's 70-year-old mother live in the household with -- of the Nikolic family, with Dusanka and Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Milenija Nikolic lived in the same household, in the Nikolic household.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Is Mrs. Milenija Nikolic retired?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She is an old-age pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Momir Nikolic's wife does?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Momir Nikolic's wife teaches literature in the Bratunac primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, would it be true to say that the salaries of those who work in education and that the pensions that old-age pensioners receive in Bosnia-Herzegovina are not very high?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Teacher's salaries and old-age pensioners' pensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina are extremely low.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, in your testimony today, you said that -- in the testimony you have given so far, you said that you studied together with Momir Nikolic, that you both returned to Bratunac and found employment there. Did you continue to see Mr. Momir Nikolic? And if you did, could you provide this Trial Chamber with more details about how you socialised, what you did, where you'd go.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: When we graduated, we both returned to Bratunac and found jobs. We continued to see each other. We would very often go to cafes together. We'd go fishing together. We'd visit each other's families. We had common friends whom we would visit, those sort of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: And your -- your friends, were they of mixed ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our circle of friends was of mixed ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Were there Muslims among your friends? That is to say, were there Bosniaks among your friends?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: When you socialised, did you ever notice that Mr. Momir Nikolic had nationalistic tendencies, with respect to ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Momir Nikolic never had any nationalistic tendencies with regard to other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to ask the usher to show the witness a document. This is a version of a document designated as document A2, which is attached to the sentencing brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, I would like to ask you -- if it's necessary to put it on the ELMO, I do have a version in English. Mr. Krsmanovic, could you please have a look at the document and read it. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, you've been Mr. Momir Nikolic's for a long time, so you could answer this question even without the document, but would it be true to say that Mr. Momir Nikolic has no previous convictions? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Momir has no previous convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to ask the usher to return those documents to me. And there is another document that I would like to show the witness. This document is designated as A3. This is the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to read this attestation as well. Mr. Krsmanovic, is it true to say that no criminal proceedings have been instituted against Mr. Momir Nikolic in Republika Srpska, no criminal proceedings for crimes of any kind have been instituted against him? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, criminal proceedings have never been instituted against Mr. Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask the usher to return the documents. I have no other documents to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, is it true to say that in -- from 1989 to 1991 there was an increase in inter-ethnic tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell Their Honours how in this period, when inter-ethnic tensions were rising among the various groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina, how Mr. Momir Nikolic behaved in that period.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Momir Nikolic was not a member of any party in that period. He behaved like a citizen who did not favour any political parties. He did not attend any political rallies. He behaved like a neutral citizen, as far as political parties were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: And did his attitude towards other nations and ethnic groups remain unchanged?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: After the end of the war and the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords, can you list the institutions and companies in which Mr. Nikolic worked?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the signing of the Dayton Accords, Mr. Nikolic first got a job in the Ministry for Displaced Persons and Refugees. After that, he was employed in a trading company called Guber. After that, he was employed in a company called Kartonaza.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Nikolic after this company was privatised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: After the privatisation of the Kartonaza company, Momir Nikolic worked there for a brief period of time, but then he was made redundant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: And how did Mr. Nikolic behave then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: After he was fired, Mr. Momir Nikolic withdrew into himself. He rarely went out, and he rarely visited the places he used to go before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: While Mr. Nikolic was the director of the Kartonaza company, did you ever hear from anyone that he embezzled any funds in that company called Kartonaza?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from anyone that any kind of investigation was carried out against Mr. Nikolic in connection with the embezzlement of some funds in that company?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, are you aware that in December 1999 Momir Nikolic gave an interview to investigators of The Hague Tribunal in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of this, because Mr. Nikolic told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what he told you on his return from that interview?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me the details, but he said the interview was long, that it was exhausting, and that he was afraid that he might be indicted for the crimes that had occurred in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the year 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, as the personal friend of Momir Nikolic, would you please tell us your opinion about the following fact: If Mr. Nikolic had known he was indicted, would he have, in your opinion, voluntarily surrendered to The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We never discussed it, but it was my impression that Momir Nikolic, had he known he was indicted, would have surrendered voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic, can you tell this Chamber on what facts you base this opinion of yours, or rather, from what facts do you draw this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can draw this conclusion from the fact that Mr. Nikolic didn't leave his home. He didn't socialise with his friends. He spent all his time either at home or close to his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Nikolic did not leave his home to go elsewhere to hide or conceal himself?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Mr. Nikolic was arrested in front of his house while he was having coffee with his 70-year-old mother and that he did not resist arrest?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was arrested close to his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are all my questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions on the side of the Prosecution? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May I ask you, where were you in the period between June and October 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Between June and October 1995, I had a work obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Jesenik timber company in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Did you have time to still meet Mr. Momir Nikolic by that time? I know it was a war and you were both of you in different appointments, but did you have time to get together some days?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, we did not socialise in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So he never made a comment to you by that time of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's question? Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender, Mr. Londrovic, through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to ask Your Honours, apart from documents marked A2 and A3, I also wish to tender all the other documents from A1 to A13. A14 is a report on Mr. Momir Nikolic's behaviour in the Detention Unit. I have no witness through whom to tender this document. I will simply ask Your Honours to admit the document marked A14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I have no question that it's -- it's a reliable document and is what counsel says it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since there's no objections, I believe that those documents are admitted into evidence. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And normally there's two ways for the parties to tender documents: One is through 92 bis; the other is through a live witness. The parties cannot tender any documents through the annex to any filings. Those annexes to the filings, just to have some reference purpose which should not be granted as any documentary or evidential value to it. Thank you. Thank you, witness, for coming to give your testimony. We all wish you have a pleasant journey back home. The usher will show you out of the courtroom. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It takes a long time to have the next witness. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I take it there's no protective measures or anything for any of the witnesses that are coming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think the counsel has informed us the first two witnesses, not to enter any protective measures. Am I right, Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the first two witnesses did not ask for my protective measures; while, the third and fourth witness did ask for protective measures, that is, for a pseudonym and image distortion. And Your Honours granted these measures at the last Status Conference, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The protective measures have been granted on the 8th of September already. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Could we have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Bozo Momcilovic, solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Mr. Kirsch, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Momcilovic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Mr. Momcilovic, just before I start, if there's any question about the questions I will ask you, if you don't understand anything, please don't hesitate to ask me and I might rephrase the question. Do you understand? Since we need an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Mr. Momcilovic, could you again please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Bozo Momcilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: I'll try to go through your personal background very quickly. It's true that you were born on the 25th of January, 1962?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: That was in Kravica, which is in Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: I understand that you're still living in Bratunac municipality? That's right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Am I right that you went to primary school in Kravica, which you finished in 1976, and then you went to the secondary school of economics in Srebrenica, which you finished in 1980?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: And after finishing the secondary school, you went to serve in the JNA for one year; that's true?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that was?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: In Rijeka, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Croatia. Thank you. What did you do after finishing your military service?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the Faculty of Economics at the University of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: And you finished there with a degree after five years? That's right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I waited for a year to find employment, and I started working in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please, where you started working then.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: In a state-owned company called Ciglana in Bratunac. This was a brickworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Are you still working in Ciglana today?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Could you please tell us for how long you worked within that firm and when you moved to another firm, which this was.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Eleven years. And in 1998, I went to work in the timber company or forestry management company in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: I'm right that you're still working there today?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Momcilovic. Now, when did you first get to know Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I first heard about Mr. Nikolic in the early '80s, and I met him in person sometime in 1988, when I started working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: So what were -- what were the circumstances when you first heard about Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about Mr. Nikolic from my friends, who went to the secondary school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you heard about Mr. Nikolic in the time then.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic was a teacher in that school, and he was teaching defence. I heard from my friends that he was a strict teacher but that he was extremely fair in the way he marked his students.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: At that time, did you hear at any time that your friends told you that Mr. Nikolic was discriminating between pupils from different ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No. I even heard that he was exceptionally correct to all children, regardless of their financial condition, their ethnic background. All he cared about was whether they had learned their lessons, not what their affiliations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: So when did you get to know Mr. Nikolic personally, then?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I met him sometime later, but I knew who he was. He didn't know what -- who I was. But then I really got to know him when I started working in the Ciglana company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: How was that? Did you have any kind of business relationship to him at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't a business relationship, but Bratunac is a small town and people with a university education all knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: So am I right that at this time you started meeting Mr. Nikolic from time to time, having a drink or having a dinner or lunch together?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: And what -- what did you learn about Mr. Nikolic's, let's say, family background at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he's married. When we met, he had a son. Later he had another son. He lived in a family house next to his father's and mother's house. I know his wife's name is Dusanka, his elder son was Brane, and his younger son was Sasa or Sale. I know that his wife is a teacher, that she teaches literature, and that in 1995 or 1996 his father died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Nikolic from time to time in this circle, were there also people from not Serb origin, meaning Croats, Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Did you hear at any time hearing Mr. Nikolic making any kind of nationalistic statement or arguing in favour of a Greater Serbia, whatever in that direction?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: So when in the period between 1989 and 1990 inter-ethnic tensions developed in the area, did you hear then of any incident Mr. Nikolic was involved, like rally or -- or whatever?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge if at that time Mr. Nikolic was a member of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDS party at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Is it true that Mr. Nikolic at that time served in the Bratunac municipality for the Territorial Defence staff?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: And was later on called to serve in the army; that's true?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: He was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Do you know in which year this was?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Nikolic did after he was demobilised? And maybe you can tell us also if you recall when that was.

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I know that in early 1996 he worked in the Ministry for Displaced Persons and Refugees, and later he became the director of the socially owned company Guber in Bratunac, and later on in 1998, he became the director of the DP Kartonaza company in Bratunac, a socially owned company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Do you know what happened after the Kartonaza company was privatised?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the new owners appointed a new director, and then Nikolic lost his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: At that time, did you meet with Mr. Nikolic from time to time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Did he ever speak to you about an interview he gave in Banja Luka, I guess it was?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: He did mention it, yes. I didn't ask him about the details. I know he went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Mr. Nikolic about -- that he was afraid maybe to be arrested because of the events that happened in Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOZO MOMCILOVIC
utterances.text: We never discussed it in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: So if the Court would allow me, I would like to ask just two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: The first is being aware of the guilty plea of Mr. Nikolic, do you think that this was a -- an important step to regain peace and to gain reconciliation in Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: I'm asking for an opinion, so I'm not sure if the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Court will allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my personal opinion, this is a positive step and requires great courage to admit one's guilt, and the Court will determine the sentence. This required courage, and I admire him for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Momcilovic. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you, witness, for coming to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And it's time for the break. I understand that the next two witnesses are under protective measures. So during the break I hope the registrar will set up the necessary preparations for the next two witnesses. And we will resume at 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. DB, the Trial Chamber has granted your request for protective measures, so your name will not be used in this courtroom to address you. We will use your pseudonym, DB, to address you. And you have -- your image has been distorted and your voice has been distorted too. Before I start putting questions to you, I would just like to ask you to wait for me to finish my question, as we both speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Londrovic, I think you have to ask some questions about the background of this witness and we could go into the private session for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I intended to do that, but I just wanted to tell the witness that he should not reply too rapidly, that -- I wanted to warn him that he should wait for the interpreters to finish interpreting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to take our exhibit marked DS15 and show it to the witness, and I would like to ask the witness to read what is contained in the document. But he should not read it out aloud. He should just confirm that this is in fact his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the document to my learned colleagues from the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber. To be of assistance to the Trial Chamber, this document has been marked TAB4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DB, could you now tell the Trial Chamber whether you know Mr. Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long you have known Mr. Momir Nikolic for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Since the '80s, since the school time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that Mr. Nikolic was your teacher in secondary school and he taught you national defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, he did, occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "occasionally", do you mean during one school year, two school years, a long or a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Half an academic year. He was working there as a substitute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: While Mr. Momir Nikolic was your teacher, did he ever demonstrate intolerance of any kind towards pupils of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Nikolic's pupils have a good opinion of him as a teacher and as a man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DB, you said that Mr. Nikolic worked as a teacher of defence. Could you tell us now who his colleagues -- who the colleagues that he would see most frequently were while he was a teacher.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: He would mostly see a colleague who taught the same subject, defence. His name was Sabid Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Is Sabid Mujkic a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DB, could you now tell us whether you know where Mr. Nikolic's house was? And if you do, could you tell us where his house is located and what the name of the place where his house is located is called.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: It is in Repovac. It's on the outskirts of the entrance to the town of Bratunac or it's on the outskirts of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnic composition of Repovac is, which is on the outskirts of Bratunac, and where Mr. Nikolic's house is located? And I'm referring to the pre-war period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: The composition of the population was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the population was mixed ethnicity, would it be correct to say that there were both Bosniaks and Serbs who lived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DB, did you ever hear anything about Mr. Momir Nikolic as a neighbour? Did he ever have any conflicts of any kind with anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No. He was never involved in any conflicts with his neighbours, not during those years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DB, did you ever have the opportunity of being in the same company with -- in Mr. Nikolic's company, in the same company with Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions, for a drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: If I say that you would go to cafes and restaurants in Bratunac, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: And the people you were with with Mr. Nikolic, were they also of mixed ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell this Trial Chamber what you would discuss on such occasions, what you would talk about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: The usual things. We didn't discuss the war then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: In the course of those conversations, did you ever feel that Mr. Nikolic demonstrated intolerance of any kind towards members of other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: No, I never noticed such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DB, are you aware of the fact that Mr. Nikolic admitted that there was a crime that was perpetrated in Srebrenica in July 1995 and that he has pleaded guilty before this Trial Chamber on a count of persecution as a crime against humanity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about this, through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DB, do you personally accept this admission of guilt, admission of responsibility on the part of Mr. Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. request us to go back into private session very briefly, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we're in the open session, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DB, do you believe that when one admits one's guilt it helps to truth to be established more rapidly, and by admitting one's guilt it is possible for the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina to become reconciled with each other more rapidly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Would you recommend that other accused admit their guilt if they feel that they are responsible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be good for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, are there any documents to tender, Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We intend to tender three other documents -- three more documents into evidence with the next -- through the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, according to your practice of these proceedings, I suggest that the document with the witness name on it should be tendered into evidence under seal, that is, the document DS15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was going to suggest this. This is Defence Exhibit DS15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there's no objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document is admitted into evidence as DS15. Well, witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will pull down the blinds and show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we are waiting for the following witness to appear, my colleague, Mr. Kirsch, has told me that this witness has been granted voice distortion, and the witness didn't request voice distortion and he only requested image distortion and protection for his name. He requested that his name be concealed. And this is also the case for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Londrovic, we only requested -- we only granted the request that the witness requested, which means -- which means there's no voice distortion but the witness will have the pseudonym and the facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then there must have been a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And how about the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness has also asked for a pseudonym to be used and has asked for facial distortion, and you granted this request at the last Status Conference. I'm not sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. DA, I would like to inform you that this Trial Chamber has granted your request for protective measures. A pseudonym will be used and you will have facial distortion. Everyone in the courtroom will use the pseudonym DA to address you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask the usher to show you this Defence exhibit, marked DS16.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Could you just have a look at the exhibit to see whether your name is written down on the document. Don't read it out aloud though. If it's correct, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the exhibit to my learned colleagues from the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber. Your Honour, could this exhibit be sealed, be presented under seal. I don't think anyone would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we go very briefly into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, can you tell us whether you know Mr. Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. I have known Momir Nikolic since secondary school through his sister Zorica, who attended primary school with me from the fifth to the eighth grade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises: Primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Nikolic finished university?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. After graduating from the secondary school of civil engineering, he graduated in national defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether Mr. Nikolic, after graduating from university, from the Faculty of National Defence, returned to Bratunac and started to work there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. After graduating from university, he came back to Bratunac and got a job at a teacher in the Bratunac secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what jobs Mr. Nikolic did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic was a teacher of general national defence in the Bratunac secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, did you socialise with Mr. Nikolic? And if you did, can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you explain in greater detail to Their Honours where and how this occurred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: As Bratunac is a small town, we would all see each other. We would often sit in the Fontana Hotel and have coffee together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: This circle of friends to which you and Mr. Nikolic belonged - and I assume there were others - was it of a mixed ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. We always sat in a circle of friends that was of a mixed ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: While you were sitting in this way, having coffee, what did you talk about mostly? What was the topic of your conversations then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: It was usually everyday topics, life in the town of Bratunac, the economy, education, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Nikolic expressing negative opinions about any nationality or ethnic group or that he advocated Greater Serbian ideas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of any such thing, and such topics were never raised in our conversations. And also, Mr. Nikolic had friends among the Muslims, the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us names, if you know, of Mr. Nikolic's good friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Mr. Pekar Dubicic [phoen]. They, as bachelors, socialised for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, while Mr. Nikolic was working as a teacher, did you ever hear that he drew distinctions among the pupils he taught, along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No, I never heard any such thing. I had close relatives who attended that school and whose teacher he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, is it true to say that in the period from 1989 to 1991 in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was an increase in inter-ethnic tensions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours how Mr. Nikolic behaved in this period of time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: In the period when the conflicts in international relations began, I never saw Mr. Nikolic at the SDS rallies or the rallies held by other political parties in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Nikolic belonged to the SDA; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: To avoid confusion, does your answer know that -- mean that he was not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: It means I'm not aware of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, are you aware of the fact that Momir Nikolic has pleaded guilty before The Hague Tribunal for the crime that occurred in Srebrenica and that he has accepted responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that, and I think that he's the first person from the Bratunac and Srebrenica area to admit guilt for the crime that happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we go back to private session very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We are looking for the English version of this letter in order to distribute it among the parties while Mr. DA is reading the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic, does this letter have a number on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the letter is marked 01-014-786/03, and it was written on the 8th of October, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to tender this letter into evidence at a later stage? Well, if so -- if so -- we'd better have a DS number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, we can mark this document as DS17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, have you read this letter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell me whether you entirely support the complete contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, I fully support the entire contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to show the witness another document, which the Defence would like to mark as Exhibit DS18. I will ask the usher to hand the English version to my learned friends and to Your Honours. I will ask the witness to pay attention to the paragraphs that have been marked in red, highlighted in red. And in order not to waste time, I will read this. It is a letter written by Mr. Emir Suljagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Prosecution hasn't been provided with this material. If we could have that. I have seen this before. I just meant I hadn't seen it in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, this is a letter written by Mr. Emir Suljagic, one of the victims of the Srebrenica crimes in 1995, and this was published in the New York Times on the 1st of June, 2003. I will ask you to pay attention to the paragraphs highlighted in red, which I will quote: "Mr. Nikolic's confession, in which he described in chilling detail how he helped organise the mass execution and burial and an extensive cover-up, all of which he says army superiors ordered him to carry out, punches a big hole in the Bosnian Serb wall of denial. Serbs should have no reason to doubt his admission. Mr. Nikolic has nothing to gain by exaggerating. I don't expect the confessions by Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic to transform Bosnian Serb views. Many of the men he named as co-conspirators are still at large. Some of them still hold senior positions in the Bosnian Serb army. One of them is a member of the parliament. But the confessions have brought me a sense of relief I have not known since the fall of Srebrenica in 1995. They have given me the acknowledgment I have been looking for these past eight years. While far from an apology, these admissions are a start. We Bosnian Muslims no longer have to prove we were victims. Our friends and cousins, fathers and brothers were killed, and we no longer have to prove they were innocent." Mr. DA, do you fully support the views expressed by Mr. Emir Suljagic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one more document, DS19. I would like to show this also to the witness. The English version may be distributed to the parties. I will ask the witness again to pay attention to the highlighted parts. This is an article entitled "Review and outlook: Revisiting Srebrenica," which was published in the Wall Street Journal Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, please pay attention to the parts I will read to you. "In a separate trial in the Srebrenica case, the testimony came about when a former Bosnian Serb intelligence chief and a brigade commander agreed to stand witness against two comrades as part of a plea bargain. In itself, that was a success. Prosecutors are finally succeeding in finding strong witnesses. Since May, eight people have made a plea bargain, compared with eight in the decade before then." "To questions by the Defence counsel why he ignored Geneva Conventions" -- I will make a digression here. This was a question put by Mr. Blagojevic's Defence counsel to Mr. Momir Nikolic as a witness: "Questioned by the defence attorney why he ignored the Geneva Conventions of war, Mr. Nikolic shot back: 'Do you really think that in an operation where 7.000 people were killed that somebody was adhering to the Geneva Conventions?' This testimony sets the dreadful record straight. Some Serbian politicians contended this massacre never took place. Now two credible Bosnian Serb witnesses explain how it happened. Some Bosnian Muslims worried that they would never know the details or see justice Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. triumph. Justice aside, at least they now know what took place. The intriguing detail of the testimony in the Srebrenica case was that the massacre was carried out by Bosnian Serb army and police, some of whom were on Belgrade's payroll. This fact alone would strengthen the already strong link between the Serbian leadership, principally Mr. Milosevic, and the thugs committing the crimes on the ground in Bosnia, where 200.000 people perished between 1992 and 1995." And would you just pay attention to the last paragraph: "The wheels of justice have turned very slowly in addressing Balkan crimes, but they are now turning faster and we are finally getting clearer testimony defining who was to blame. The next question is whether Serbia's new leaders will accept their responsibility to help round up the suspects still at large and deliver them to The Hague." Mr. DA, my last question to you is: Do you fully support everything I have read out and do you support these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, fully. I support all this fully, and I stand by this conclusion. The admission by Momir Nikolic has opened up all these processes about the crimes that happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DA, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I have a question to ask you: Do you know Mr. Nikolic served in the capacity of the chief of the department of the Ministry for Refugees and Displaced Persons in Bratunac and as a co-coordinator of the Ministry of the Municipality following his demobilisation in April 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this. I came to Bratunac in 1998. But I do know that he was the director of a company called Kartonaza in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what was the reaction of the Serbian community to the -- Mr. Nikolic's guilty plea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: It was not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's question? It seems to me there's none. Yes, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Londrovic. Further questioned by Mr. Londrovic:

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. DA, you said the reaction of the Serbs to Mr. Momir Nikolic's guilty plea was not good.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is there a part of the Serb community which considers Mr. Momir Nikolic a traitor of Serbian interests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's what they think.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to talk to individual Serbs who condemn Mr. Nikolic's guilty plea and his admission of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to finish that one point, are you aware of any Serbs that supported Mr. Nikolic's guilty plea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to tender the following documents as Defence exhibits: DS16, DS17, DS18, and DS19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These four documents are admitted into evidence. Well, witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, she will take you out of this courtroom. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have finished the witnesses called by the Defence team. Mr. Londrovic, are you going to make any statement at this stage? Of course, at the end of the proceedings, which means tomorrow afternoon probably, the parties, both parties will have the right to make closing statements. Anyway, if you want to make any statements at this stage, you may do so, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. At this point, I have nothing to say. At the end, Mr. Nikolic's Defence will present its closing arguments and say everything it feels is relevant and important for the sentencing of Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, tomorrow afternoon we'll hear the Rule 98 witnesses. There are three witnesses called by this Trial Chamber. The purpose for calling those witnesses is to assess the cooperation between Mr. Nikolic and the Prosecution and not due to concern about lack of the factual basis to support the guilty plea and subsequent conviction. I want to make this very clear to both parties. This Trial Chamber has made three confidential orders concerning with these three witnesses in this proceeding. In each order, we defined very clearly the scope of the areas that we would like to ask some questions to those witnesses. I hope both parties will function within those scopes defined in those three orders. The procedure is that the witness may summarise his previous statements or the Trial Chamber may ask some questions to those witnesses. Then the parties could ask some questions to that witness. But all the questions should be within the scope defined in our orders. Are there any questions concerning of the procedure for tomorrow's proceedings? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President. I did just want to make it clear for the record that one of those witnesses the Prosecution has spoken to as a -- as a Prosecution witness and -- and -- about this -- about the subject matter of the entire case, including the subject matter that the Court was interested in, as I'm sure counsel is aware. The other two witnesses the Prosecution has not spoken to, nor do they intend to speak to at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your information. Mr. Londrovic, any questions? Concerning with tomorrow's proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour, but I wish to clarify the procedure. As far as I understood you, the witness will first make a statement, then Your Honours may question him, and then I assume the order is as follows: The witness may be questioned by the Prosecution, my learned friends, and finally by the Defence. Would you please confirm whether I'm right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe so. Most of what you said is right, but sometimes a witness is reluctant to make any statement at first, and maybe we'll begin by questions asked by the Judges so that is more direct and that will give the proper guidance to the witness and tell him the scope of the questions. Maybe we will begin with the questions asked by the Judges tomorrow, and then the Prosecution will ask some questions, and the Defence also could ask some questions. Yes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no problems with any of that; though I would -- if the Court would consider, I have not spoken to counsel about this, but perhaps it would be more appropriate that the Defence start with the cross-examination of these witnesses, since it is their -- their client at sentencing. I may not have much to cross-examine on, and we could save time, as opposed to me wondering how much I should cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- well, Mr. McCloskey, those witnesses are Court witnesses. In the civil law system, I think the Judge will ask the questions mainly. I don't think there is a strict line between the direct examination or cross-examination. I think everything could be very flexible. If you do not want to ask a question after Judges' questions, then maybe the Defence could ask the question first. We just want to give you an opportunity to -- to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I would like to take you up on that opportunity, and especially try to bring out any problems in the testimony or any untruthful situations. I'm just saying I may be -- we may be able to save more time if I do that second, as opposed to first. But I can discuss that with counsel too to see, and we're flexible obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. And Mr. Londrovic, I understand your client wants to make a statement at the end of the proceedings. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are right. Mr. Momir Nikolic, after the closing arguments by his Defence counsel, intends to briefly address the Chamber, and this will not take longer than ten minutes, in our estimation. The essence of what he intends is to publicly express his remorse once again and to say that he spoke the absolute truth and to explain the reasons for his guilty plea and the reason why he accepted responsibility for the crimes that occurred after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, I have to tell you that after Mr. Nikolic's statement, the Chamber may ask him some questions, which of course will not go to the -- the convictions but only concerning with the cooperations. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully understand that, and I think my client understands that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Well, this afternoon we are ahead of time, so we are adjourned until 3.00, tomorrow afternoon.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.05 p.m.
